strengths: The proposed repair of problematic seam segments addresses a practical stitching failure. Local realignment followed by boundary-constrained seam recomputation is a sensible, modular approach.
Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets. Figures 1, 10, and 11 show convincing improvements to discontinuous curbs, paving, and stairs.

The user study provides supporting perceptual evidence: the proposed method receives 108 of 160 first-place votes. Reported timings also suggest substantially less overhead than iterative seam estimation [17] on difficult examples.

The high-level pipeline, pseudocode, and principal parameter settings are understandable, and the constituent methods and public datasets are attributed. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 usefully acknowledge failures under extensive misalignment and large residual displacement.
weaknesses: The advance over closely related alignment-refining approaches is insufficiently established. Most ingredients come from existing seam evaluation, SIFT flow, and graph-cut methods. Quantitative comparisons cover only seam-cutting methods [16,17]; comparisons with seam-driven methods [18,26] are limited to selected visual examples. The cited residual-warping approach [12] is not evaluated. These omissions leave the significance of the incremental contribution uncertain.

The central flow modification is not specified precisely enough. Section 3.4 writes the modified displacement as f(V), but Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of spatial coordinate t, without explicitly defining its application to the displacement vector. An x-dependent taper alone does not establish compatibility around the entire rectangular patch boundary. Handling overlapping repair patches and unreliable correspondences is also unclear, weakening reproducibility and the assertion that repair cannot worsen results.

There are no systematic component ablations. Figure 4 illustrates several sigmoid settings on one patch, but does not establish the separate benefits of adaptive patch selection, flow modification, and constrained seam merging across datasets. Experiments also use only alignment method [15] and initial seam method [16], leaving the claimed general applicability untested.

The quantitative quality evidence is narrow. Equation (5) closely follows the SSIM criterion used to identify repair regions and measures seam agreement rather than overall geometric or perceptual fidelity. The manuscript itself reports disagreement with visual quality on SEAGULL pair 17. The user study helps, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples, without per-example results or a documented presentation-randomization procedure, provide limited evidence of general perceptual superiority.

The claim that the approach can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes small local parallax, while the relative test max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) can accept a uniformly high-error seam. The acknowledged limitations appropriately narrow the method to localized residual repair, but experiments do not characterize performance versus residual displacement or the extent of misalignment.

Several reporting errors require correction: Figures 6, 8, and 9 label baselines as [21]/[19], inconsistent with the methods described in the text, and Table 1 contains 159 and 161 rankings for the two baselines rather than 160 each. These appear correctable and are secondary to the methodological and experimental concerns.
